reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / KDIGO CKD-MBD guidance
clinicalPearls: A life-threatening small-vessel disorder in which calcification of dermal and subcutaneous arterioles causes ischaemia, necrosis, and ulceration
Occurs most often in patients with end-stage kidney disease on dialysis, but a non-uraemic form also exists
Presents with exquisitely painful, indurated plaques that evolve into retiform (net-like) purpura and black necrotic ulcers with a firm surrounding rim
Lesions favour areas of greater adiposity such as the thighs, abdomen, and buttocks, where prognosis is worse than for distal (acral) disease
Recognised risk factors include disordered calcium-phosphate metabolism and hyperparathyroidism, obesity, diabetes, female sex, warfarin use, and protein C or S deficiency
Secondary wound infection and sepsis are the leading causes of death, so severe pain out of proportion to visible changes should prompt early suspicion

Management is multidisciplinary and includes correction of calcium-phosphate imbalance and hyperparathyroidism, sodium thiosulfate, meticulous wound care, analgesia, and avoidance of precipitants such as warfarin
reference.pathophysiology: Calciphylaxis is driven by progressive calcification of the media of small dermal and subcutaneous arterioles, accompanied by intimal fibrosis and microthrombosis, which occludes the vessels and causes ischaemic necrosis of skin and fat. In the uraemic form, chronic kidney disease with a deranged calcium-phosphate product, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and reduced levels of circulating calcification inhibitors allow vascular smooth-muscle cells to transform into an osteoblast-like, calcifying phenotype. A hypercoagulable tendency, exacerbated by warfarin's inhibition of vitamin-K-dependent calcification inhibitors, promotes the thrombotic occlusion that completes tissue infarction.
additionalDifferentials: Antiphospholipid syndrome and other thrombotic microangiopathies
Peripheral arterial disease with ischaemic ulceration
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy (used judiciously given ulceration risk) showing medial arteriolar calcification, intimal fibrosis, and thrombosis
Serum calcium, phosphate, calcium-phosphate product, and parathyroid hormone
Renal function and dialysis adequacy assessment
Coagulation studies and screening for protein C or S deficiency and antiphospholipid antibodies
Review of warfarin and other precipitant medications
Imaging such as plain radiographs or bone scintigraphy that may reveal soft-tissue vascular calcification
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging necrotic ulcers with surrounding cellulitis and systemic sepsis
Severe pain disproportionate to visible skin changes signalling early disease
Truncal or proximal (central) lesions carrying a worse prognosis
Signs of overwhelming infection in an immunocompromised or dialysis-dependent patient
reference.prognosis: The condition carries high morbidity and mortality, with sepsis from infected necrotic wounds the usual cause of death; central and ulcerated lesions fare worse than distal non-ulcerated disease, though early multidisciplinary intervention can improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Dismissing severe pain before ulceration appears and delaying diagnosis
Continuing warfarin, which aggravates the disease, when an alternative anticoagulant may be appropriate
Aggressive debridement or biopsy that can extend non-healing wounds if not carefully weighed
Failing to address the underlying calcium-phosphate and parathyroid derangement
references: KDIGO clinical practice guidance on CKD-mineral and bone disorder
management: Correct the mineral-bone derangement: lower phosphate with non-calcium-based binders, avoid calcium-containing binders and excess vitamin D, and treat hyperparathyroidism with cinacalcet or parathyroidectomy.
Give intravenous sodium thiosulfate as targeted therapy for the calcific arteriolopathy.
Stop warfarin and switch to an alternative anticoagulant, and withdraw other precipitants such as calcium and vitamin D loading.
Optimise dialysis, often intensifying the regimen, in end-stage kidney disease.
Provide meticulous wound care, surgical debridement where appropriate, and aggressive multimodal analgesia for the severe pain.
Treat wound infection promptly with antibiotics, recognising sepsis as the leading cause of death.
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across nephrology, dermatology, wound care, pain and surgical teams.
